marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q015.takeaway: Hairpin loops of end arteries are prominent in the metaphysis, a highly vascular growth region.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q015.displayText:
Hairpin loops of end arteries are prominent in the metaphysis, a highly vascular growth region.

Hairpin bends of end arteries are seen abundantly in the metaphysis.

The metaphysis is the portion of a long bone between epiphysis and diaphysis. It is the zone of active growth and is highly vascular. Before epiphysial fusion, it is richly supplied through end arteries forming hairpin bends.

The metaphysis is the most common location for osteomyelitis in children because bacteria or emboli are easily trapped in these hairpin bends.
emphasis: Hairpin loops of end arteries are prominent in the metaphysis, a highly vascular growth region

rationales.a: The epiphysis has a separate epiphyseal circulation; hairpin loops are characteristic of metaphysis.
rationales.c: The diaphysis receives the nutrient artery and cortical branches rather than abundant metaphyseal hairpin loops.
rationales.d: The growth plate itself is avascular cartilage, unlike the vascular metaphysis.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q016.takeaway: Articular cartilage lacks perichondrium, although most other hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage types follow the listed pattern.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q016.displayText:
Articular cartilage lacks perichondrium, although most other hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage types follow the listed pattern.

Articular cartilage, despite being a type of hyaline cartilage, lacks perichondrium.

Cartilage is connective tissue composed of chondrocytes and fibers (collagen or yellow elastic fibers) embedded in a firm gel-like mucopolysaccharide-rich matrix. It is more elastic than bone, has no blood vessels or lymphatics, and chondrocytes are nourished by diffusion. Cartilage has no nerves and is insensitive.

There are three types: hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage. Hyaline cartilage except articular cartilage, and elastic cartilage, have perichondrium; fibrocartilage does not.
emphasis: Articular cartilage lacks perichondrium, although most other hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage types follow the listed pattern

rationales.a: Most hyaline cartilage has a perichondrium, except articular surfaces and epiphyseal plates.
rationales.d: Elastic cartilage is ordinarily surrounded by perichondrium.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q017.takeaway: Nasal septal cartilage is hyaline; elastic (yellow) cartilage occurs in the pinna, epiglottis and arytenoid apex.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q017.displayText:
Nasal septal cartilage is hyaline; elastic (yellow) cartilage occurs in the pinna, epiglottis and arytenoid apex.

The septal nasal cartilage has hyaline cartilage and not yellow (elastic) cartilage.

Elastic/yellow cartilage contains a matrix rich in fine yellow elastic fibers containing elastin. It is present in apices of arytenoid, epiglottis, corniculate cartilages, cuneiform cartilages, Eustachian tube, pinna (auricle), and external auditory meatus.
emphasis: Nasal septal cartilage is hyaline; elastic (yellow) cartilage occurs in the pinna, epiglottis and arytenoid apex

rationales.a: The epiglottis is composed mainly of elastic cartilage.
rationales.c: The apex of the arytenoid is an example of elastic cartilage.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q018.takeaway: The pubic symphysis contains fibrocartilage between the pubic bones.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q018.displayText:
The pubic symphysis contains fibrocartilage between the pubic bones.

The structure marked X is the pubic symphysis and the cartilage is fibrocartilage.

Fibrocartilage contains a mixture of white fibrous tissue and cartilaginous tissue, making it extremely tough and resilient. Sites include pubic symphysis, manubriosternal joint, articular discs of temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints, anulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs, menisci of knee, acetabular labrum, glenoid labrum, and lining of bony grooves for tendons.
emphasis: The pubic symphysis contains fibrocartilage between the pubic bones

rationales.a: The pubic symphysis is not hyaline cartilage; its interpubic disc is fibrocartilaginous.
rationales.b: Calcification may occur in cartilage with age, but the normal symphyseal disc is fibrocartilage.
rationales.d: Elastic cartilage is found in structures such as the pinna, not the pubic symphysis.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q019.takeaway: Fibrocartilage is rich in type I collagen, giving it tensile strength under compression and shear.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q019.displayText:
Fibrocartilage is rich in type I collagen, giving it tensile strength under compression and shear.

Fibrocartilage predominantly contains type I collagen. Hyaline and elastic cartilages mainly contain type II collagen.
emphasis: Fibrocartilage is rich in type I collagen, giving it tensile strength under compression and shear

rationales.a: Reticular tissue is built from type III collagen reticular fibers, not predominantly type I cartilage matrix.
rationales.c: Elastic cartilage has type II collagen with abundant elastin fibers.
rationales.d: Basement membranes are rich in type IV collagen, not type I.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q020.takeaway: Ligamentum flavum contains abundant elastin, which lets it recoil after spinal flexion.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q020.displayText:
Ligamentum flavum contains abundant elastin, which lets it recoil after spinal flexion.

Ligamentum flavum has high levels of elastin fibres.

The ligamenta flava are ligaments connecting the ventral parts of the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. They predominantly contain elastic tissue and form part of the posterior surface of the vertebral canal. Their high elastin content allows stretching by 80% without damage. They resist separation of laminae in flexion and assist extension back to anatomical position.
emphasis: Ligamentum flavum contains abundant elastin, which lets it recoil after spinal flexion

rationales.a: Type I collagen is abundant in many ligaments, but elastin predominates in ligamenta flava.
rationales.b: Type II collagen is typical of cartilage, not the elastic spinal ligament.
rationales.c: Reticular fibers form supporting networks in lymphoid organs and do not dominate ligamentum flavum.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q021.takeaway: A symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q021.displayText:
A symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous joint.

The symphysis is not a fibrous joint, but a secondary cartilaginous joint.
emphasis: A symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous joint

rationales.a: Cranial sutures are fibrous joints joined by dense connective tissue.
rationales.b: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint linked by ligament or interosseous membrane.
rationales.d: Gomphosis is a fibrous peg-and-socket joint between tooth and alveolus.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q022.takeaway: Synovial joints are freely movable and functionally classified as diarthroses.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q022.displayText:
Synovial joints are freely movable and functionally classified as diarthroses.

Synovial joints are freely movable joints and are therefore functionally classified as diarthroses.

Functional classification: synarthroses are immovable, e.g. fibrous joints; amphiarthroses are slightly mobile, e.g. cartilaginous joints; diarthroses are freely mobile, e.g. synovial joints.
emphasis: Synovial joints are freely movable and functionally classified as diarthroses

rationales.a: Synarthroses are immovable joints, commonly fibrous.
rationales.b: Amphiarthroses allow slight movement and commonly include symphyses.
rationales.d: Syndesmosis names a structural fibrous joint, not a functional movement class.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q023.takeaway: A joint with three or more articulating surfaces is compound; complex joints contain an articular disc or meniscus.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q023.displayText:
A joint with three or more articulating surfaces is compound; complex joints contain an articular disc or meniscus.

A joint with three or more articular surfaces is classified as a compound joint.

Classification by number of articulating surfaces: simple joints have 2 surfaces (e.g. shoulder, hip); compound joints have 3 or more surfaces (e.g. elbow, wrist); complex joints have an intra-articular disc between articular surfaces dividing the joint space (e.g. temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints).
emphasis: A joint with three or more articulating surfaces is compound; complex joints contain an articular disc or meniscus

rationales.a: A simple joint has only two articular surfaces.
rationales.b: Complex refers to a disc or meniscus dividing the joint cavity, not the number of surfaces alone.
rationales.c: Synarthrosis describes movement, not the count of articular surfaces.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q024.takeaway: Gomphosis is the fibrous peg-and-socket joint anchoring a tooth in its alveolus.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q024.displayText:
Gomphosis is the fibrous peg-and-socket joint anchoring a tooth in its alveolus.

Gomphosis (dentoalveolar syndesmosis) is a peg-and-socket joint between a tooth and its socket.

Fibrous joints are joints where bones are joined by fibrous tissue and are classified as sutures, syndesmosis and gomphosis.
emphasis: Gomphosis is the fibrous peg-and-socket joint anchoring a tooth in its alveolus

rationales.a: Syndesmosis joins bones by a ligament or membrane, not a tooth-in-socket peg.
rationales.c: A hinge joint permits uniaxial flexion-extension.
rationales.d: A pivot joint permits rotation around an axis.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q025.takeaway: The incudostapedial articulation is a small ball-and-socket synovial joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q025.displayText:
The incudostapedial articulation is a small ball-and-socket synovial joint.

The incudostapedial joint is a ball-and-socket type of joint.

In ball-and-socket joints a globular head (male surface) fits a cup-shaped socket (female surface). They are multiaxial and allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, medial rotation, lateral rotation and circumduction. Examples include shoulder, hip, talocalcaneonavicular and incudostapedial joints.

Note: the other joint between incus and malleus (incudomalleolar joint) is a saddle joint.
emphasis: The incudostapedial articulation is a small ball-and-socket synovial joint

rationales.a: A saddle joint has reciprocally concave-convex surfaces; this is not the incudostapedial form.
rationales.b: A hinge joint permits flexion-extension around one axis, unlike this ossicular articulation.
rationales.d: A pivot joint rotates around a central axis and does not describe incudostapedial surfaces.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q026.takeaway: The first metatarsophalangeal joint is ellipsoid; hallux valgus is lateral deviation at this joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q026.displayText:
The first metatarsophalangeal joint is ellipsoid; hallux valgus is lateral deviation at this joint.

The deformity shown is hallux valgus, caused by excessive lateral deviation at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. It is an example of an ellipsoid joint.

Ellipsoid joints have an oval convex (male) surface fitting an elliptical concave (female) surface and show biaxial flexion-extension and abduction-adduction; combined movements produce circumduction, while movement around a third axis is prevented by articular shape. Examples include wrist/radiocarpal, atlanto-occipital, metacarpophalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints.
emphasis: The first metatarsophalangeal joint is ellipsoid; hallux valgus is lateral deviation at this joint

rationales.a: The first metatarsophalangeal joint is not a pivot joint; it permits flexion-extension and abduction-adduction.
rationales.b: Saddle joints have reciprocal surfaces, as at the thumb carpometacarpal joint.
rationales.d: A hinge joint is uniaxial; the metatarsophalangeal joint is biaxial/ellipsoid.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q027.takeaway: The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball-and-socket articulation centered on the head of the talus.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q027.displayText:
The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball-and-socket articulation centered on the head of the talus.

The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball-and-socket joint.

The ball is the rounded head of talus. The socket is formed by the posterior surface of navicular, anterior articular surface of calcaneus, and upper surface of the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament.
emphasis: The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball-and-socket articulation centered on the head of the talus

rationales.b: The joint is not a saddle; the talar head forms a rounded ball in a socket.
rationales.c: A plane joint has nearly flat surfaces with gliding movement, unlike this multi-surface articulation.
rationales.d: An ellipsoid joint has an oval convex surface, not the spherical talar head here.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q028.takeaway: Forward and backward mandibular movements are protraction and retraction, respectively.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q028.displayText:
Forward and backward mandibular movements are protraction and retraction, respectively.

Forward and backward movement of the mandible at the temporomandibular joints are protraction and retraction, respectively. Protraction pushes the lower jaw forward; retraction pulls it backward.

Protraction and retraction also occur in the scapula: protraction moves the scapula laterally and anteriorly along the chest wall, while retraction brings it back after protraction.

Opposition brings the thumb tip into contact with a fingertip; return is reposition. Excursion is side-to-side movement of the mandible. Depression and elevation are downward and upward movements of mandible or scapula, respectively.
emphasis: Forward and backward mandibular movements are protraction and retraction, respectively

rationales.a: Opposition/reposition describe thumb movements, not mandibular translation.
rationales.b: Excursion may describe lateral jaw movement, while incursion is not the named forward-backward pair.
rationales.d: Depression/elevation mean opening and closing the jaw vertically.
